A.explanation: Matches $F = P/v$ with constant $P$, so $F$ is large at small $v$ and falls as $1/v$ as $v$ increases.

B.explanation: A straight line through the origin is $F$ proportional to $v$, which would make $P = Fv$ proportional to $v^2$, not constant.

C.explanation: Shows $F$ increasing with $v$ and levelling off, whereas constant power requires $F$ to decrease when $v$ increases.

D.explanation: Shows $F$ increasing ever more steeply with $v$, which would make $P = Fv$ increase rapidly, not stay constant.

hints: Notice the condition is constant power $P$, not constant force, while the axes are $F$ against $v$.
Recall the driving-power relation $P = Fv$ for force in the direction of velocity.
Rearrange to $F = P/v$ with $P$ constant and ask which $F$-$v$ curve falls as $1/v$.
walkthrough: Identify the governing rule for mechanical power: $P = Fv$ when the applied force $F$ acts in the direction of velocity $v$.
The question states $P$ is kept constant while $v$ increases, so rearrange to $F = P/v$.
This is an inverse proportion: doubling $v$ must halve $F$ to keep the product $Fv$ fixed.
On an $F$ against $v$ graph this gives a rectangular hyperbola that starts high at small $v$ and decreases with a decreasing gradient toward zero.
Graphs B, C and D all show $F$ increasing with $v$, so they would give increasing $P = Fv$.
Only the decreasing $1/v$ curve has the required shape. This is option A.
